chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: EM Algorithm for Semi-Supervised Naive Bayes
content:
\textbf{Input:} labeled examples $L$ with known class and attribute values, unlabeled examples $U$ with only attribute values

\textbf{Output:} class priors $P(C_k)$, attribute likelihoods $P(A_i\mid C_k)$, and soft labels for $U$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Using only $L$, estimate initial priors $P(C_k)$ and likelihoods $P(A_i\mid C_k)$ exactly as in ordinary Naive Bayes (Section 2.2).
\item \textbf{E-step:} for every unlabeled example $x\in U$, compute the (unnormalized) score $P(C_k)\prod_i P(A_i\mid C_k)$ for each class $C_k$, then normalize these scores to sum to $1$ — this gives the soft label $P(C_k\mid x)$.
\item \textbf{M-step:} recompute every prior and likelihood using both the labeled data (weight $1$ per example) and every unlabeled example (weighted by its soft label from step 2) as fractional counts.
\item If the parameters changed from the previous round, go back to step 2; otherwise stop.
\item Return the final parameters and the final soft labels for $U$.
\end{enumerate}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Semi-Supervised Learning with the EM Algorithm
title: Why EM Helps Here: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Using
content:
\textbf{Why EM Helps Here:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Using $L$ alone (Example 4.4) gives parameters based on only 6 examples
\item EM lets the unlabeled example $U_1$ contribute information too, \textbf{proportional to how confident} the model currently is about its class (Example 4.5), rather than guessing a hard label
\item After the M-step (Example 4.6), the parameters shift slightly — toward whichever class the soft label favored more (here, No shifted up because $U_1$ was $66.7\%$ likely No)
\item With a large unlabeled set $U$, this fractional-counting process can noticeably sharpen a classifier trained from only a small labeled set $L$
\end{enumerate}

section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Core RL Terminology: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Agent the
content:
\textbf{Core RL Terminology:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item \textbf{Agent} the learner or decision maker
\item \textbf{Environment} everything the agent interacts with and that responds to its actions
\item \textbf{State $s_t$} a description of the situation at time $t$
\item \textbf{Action $a_t$} a choice the agent makes at time $t$
\item \textbf{Reward $r_t$} a numerical signal received after taking an action, indicating how good or bad the outcome was
\item \textbf{Policy} the agent's strategy for choosing an action given a state
\end{enumerate}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Discounted Return
content:
The return $G_t$ is the total reward the agent collects from time $t$ onward, with rewards further in the future counted for less using a \textbf{discount factor} $\gamma$ where $0 \le \gamma < 1$:
\[
G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \gamma^2 r_{t+3} + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}
\]

This is the same geometric-series idea used in compound interest, just applied to rewards shrinking into the future instead of money growing.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Computing Discounted Return
content:
\textbf{Input:} a sequence of rewards $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ received after time $t$, discount factor $\gamma$

\textbf{Output:} the discounted return $G_t$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Multiply the first reward $r_1$ by $\gamma^0=1$.
\item Multiply the second reward $r_2$ by $\gamma^1$.
\item Continue multiplying each subsequent reward $r_k$ by $\gamma^{k-1}$.
\item Sum all the discounted rewards to obtain $G_t$.
\end{enumerate}

section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Markov Chain
content: A Markov chain is a system that moves between a fixed set of \textbf{states} over time, where the transition to the next state depends only on probabilities attached to the current state. Every possible transition is described by a \textbf{transition probability} $P(s_{t+1}=j \mid s_t=i)$.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Computing the Probability of a State Sequence
content:
\textbf{Input:} a transition probability table, a known starting state, an ordered sequence of future states

\textbf{Output:} the probability of observing exactly that sequence of states

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Start with probability $1$ at the given starting state.
\item For each step in the sequence, multiply the running probability by the transition probability from the current state to the next state in the sequence.
\item Move to the next state and repeat step 2 until the sequence ends.
\item Return the final product as the probability of the sequence.
\end{enumerate}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Reinforcement Learning and Hidden Markov Models
title: Computing the Joint Probability of a Hidden State Path and an Observation Sequence
content:
\textbf{Input:} initial probabilities $\pi$, transition probabilities $A$, emission probabilities $B$, a specific hidden state sequence, an observation sequence of the same length

\textbf{Output:} the joint probability $P(\text{states, observations})$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Start with $\pi(\text{first state})$.
\item Multiply by the emission probability of the first observation given the first state.
\item For every following time step, multiply by the transition probability from the previous state to the current state, then multiply by the emission probability of the current observation given the current state.
\item Return the final product.
\end{enumerate}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Markov Decision Process (MDP)
content:
A Markov Decision Process formally models an RL environment using five components $(S,A,P,R,\gamma)$: a set of \textbf{states} $S$, a set of \textbf{actions} $A$, \textbf{transition probabilities} $P(s'\mid s,a)$ of reaching state $s'$ after taking action $a$ in state $s$, a \textbf{reward function} $R(s,a,s')$, and a \textbf{discount factor} $\gamma$. The Markov property (Section 4.2.2) applies here too: the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the full history.

This combines the Markov chain of Section 4.2.2 (states and transitions) with the actions and rewards of reinforcement learning (Section 4.2.1) into one formal framework.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: State-Value Function
content:
The value $V^\pi(s)$ of a state $s$ under policy $\pi$ is the expected discounted return obtained by starting in $s$ and following $\pi$ thereafter. For a deterministic environment (each action leads to exactly one next state), it satisfies the \textbf{Bellman equation}:
\[
V^\pi(s) = R(s,\pi(s),s') + \gamma\, V^\pi(s')
\]
where $s'$ is the state reached from $s$ by taking action $\pi(s)$.

This is simply the discounted-return idea from Section 4.2.1 written \textit{recursively}: the value of a state is this step's reward plus the (discounted) value of wherever you land next.

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: Computing State Values by Backward Induction (Deterministic MDP)
content:
\textbf{Input:} states, one deterministic transition and reward per action, discount factor $\gamma$, a known terminal state

\textbf{Output:} $V(s)$ for every state

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Set $V(\text{terminal state}) = 0$.
\item Identify a state $s$ whose next state's value is already known.
\item Compute $V(s) = R(s,a,s') + \gamma V(s')$ for the action $a$ that will be taken from $s$.
\item Repeat steps 2 to 3, working backward, until every state has a computed value.
\item Return all computed values.
\end{enumerate}

chapter: Chapter 4 - Semi-Supervised Learning and Reinforcement Learning
section: Markov Decision Processes
title: MDP Summary — How Everything in
content:
\textbf{MDP Summary — How Everything in This Chapter Connects:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item The \textbf{discounted return} $G_t$ (Section 4.2.1) is what a value function $V(s)$ tries to predict \textit{in expectation} from state $s$ onward
\item The \textbf{Bellman equation} rewrites that return recursively, one step at a time, instead of summing the whole future at once
\item \textbf{Monte Carlo} (Section 4.3) estimates $V(s)$ by averaging actual sampled returns; backward induction here computes $V(s)$ exactly when the model (transitions and rewards) is fully known
\item The \textbf{exploration-exploitation} trade-off (Section 4.4) arises precisely because an agent usually does \textbf{not} know $P$, $R$, or the true value function in advance, and must learn them through interaction
\end{enumerate}
